newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Talk of video disc format war premature - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Talk of video disc format war premature - analysts.

text.p: Analysts said on Thursday it was premature to predict an apparent split over the development of digital video discs (DVDs) would flare into a war, blighting the market for the promising new product.

Although Sony Corp and Philips Electronics seemed to have turned their backs on the other members of a group which agreed a common format for recordable DVDs (DVD-RAM) in April, a common standard may yet emerge, they said.
Sony, Philips and Hewlett-Packard Co are seeking the approval of computer-makers for a different format for recordable DVD discs, Sony said on Wednesday.
DVDs -- also known as digital versatile discs -- are widely viewed as an important new product for the consumer electronics and computer markets.
They offer far greater storage capacity than conventional audio compact discs, computer CD ROMs and video tapes which they are eventually expected to replace.
Press reports have suggested the Sony/Philips move could spark a battle between rival DVD formats, much like the competing VHS and Betamax video systems in the early 1980s.
But analysts said such talk was premature as the original group of 10 companies might still agree on one format.

"The (press) coverage has been a bit exaggerated...I would view it as a negotiating tactic. I would still expect a common standard at the end of the day," said analyst Simon Street of Barclays de Zoete Wedd in London.
"It is a proposal (by Sony and Philips), not a fait accompli," he added.
Angela Dean, analyst at Morgan Stanley, said she was disappointed by the news of the apparent rift but was not surprised, given the long history of quibbling over DVD standards.
"This is disappointing but it should not be overplayed because tomorrow we could have an announcement saying they are all quite happy and they've got together again," she said.
Dean agreed there might be an element of posturing in the move by Sony and Philips, noting that in the past Philips had been keen to establish a broad consensus on DVD.
Analysts said DVD could become an important product once it was rolled out and established all over the world.
A common standard could help, as illustrated by the growth of the digital cellular phone market in Europe where the common GSM standard is used while the U.S. still has competing systems.
